key: Lo! I, even I, am thy Lord, So take off thy shoes, for lo! thou art in the holy valley of Tuwa.
s: Early in Ta-Ha, Moses reaches the fire and is called by name; al-Tabari, on 20:11 to 20:12, reads the command as letting his bare feet touch the blessing of a sanctified valley, since nothing in the text ties it to sandals of donkey skin.

evidence.words: وأولى القولين في ذلك بالصواب قول من قال: أمره الله تعالى ذكره بخلع نعليه ليباشر بقدميه بركة الوادي، إذ كان واديا مقدسا. وإنما قلنا ذلك أولى التأويلين بالصواب، لأنه لا دلالة في ظاهر التنزيل على أنه أمر بخلعهما من أجل أنهما من جلد حمار ولا لنجاستهما
evidence.gloss: The more correct of the two views is that of those who said: God commanded him to take off his sandals so that his feet might touch the blessing of the valley directly, since it was a holy valley. We call that the more correct interpretation because nothing in the plain wording of the revelation indicates that he was told to take them off because they were of donkey skin, nor because they were unclean.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Ta-Ha 20:12, at 2359). Opened al-Tabari on 20:11 to 20:12 (one segment) through packet.js, and read Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and the Jalalayn headings for the day. Al-Tabari reports two views (dead donkey skin, from Kaʿb, ʿIkrima, Qatada, ʿAli; direct contact with the blessed ground, from al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Abi Najih) and in his own voice prefers the second, giving as reason that nothing in the outward text ties the command to donkey skin or impurity and that ‘thou art in the holy valley’ follows as clear evidence; he also doubts the isnad of the Ibn Masʿud hadith on the donkey-skin sandals. The sentence paraphrases his preference and his first reason without drift. Plain sense draws on 20:10 to 20:11, not the key verse. Entry-check ok.
